blocks.content: The Relational Database Design module covered how to identify entities, keys, and relationships and turn them into a working schema, this new module, Normalization, covers a formal process for refining that schema further, removing redundancy that causes real, concrete problems.

This topic covers exactly what goes wrong in a schema that has not been normalized, three specific categories of anomaly, and previews the sequence of normal forms the rest of this module walks through one at a time.

1. What an Unnormalized Table Looks Like
blocks.text: 1. What an Unnormalized Table Looks Like

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438609591-570517996.png
blocks.alt: What an Unnormalized Table Looks Like

blocks.content: Suppose an orders table stores the customer name and email directly in every single order row, instead of referencing a separate customers table, every time that customer places another order, their name and email get repeated all over again, this repetition is the starting symptom of an unnormalized design.

-- Unnormalized: customer info repeated in every order row
order_id | customer_name | customer_email      | product
1        | Aisha Khan     | aisha@example.com   | Laptop
2        | Aisha Khan     | aisha@example.com   | Mouse

blocks.content: 2. Update Anomalies
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438609591-736204936.png

When the same customer email is repeated across many rows, updating it correctly means updating every single one of those rows, missing even one leaves the data inconsistent, some rows showing the old email and some showing the new one, this is called an update anomaly.

{"headers":["Anomaly Type","What Goes Wrong"],"rows":[["Update anomaly","Repeated data updated in some rows but missed in others"],["Insertion anomaly","Cannot record a fact until an unrelated fact also exists"]]}
3. Insertion Anomalies
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438609591-954143268.png

If product details only exist as columns on the orders table, adding a brand new product to the catalog before it has ever been ordered becomes awkward, or outright impossible, since there is no order row to attach that product information to yet, this is an insertion anomaly.
4. Deletion Anomalies
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438609592-630369414.png

If customer information only lives inside order rows, deleting a customer last remaining order deletes their contact information along with it, even though the customer themselves should still exist as a record, this is a deletion anomaly, losing information that was never meant to depend on that specific row.

blocks.title: All three anomalies share one root cause
blocks.content: Update, insertion, and deletion anomalies all stem from the same underlying problem, storing a fact that is genuinely about one entity, a customer, a product, inside a table that is really about a different entity, an order.
5. Normalization vs a Properly Split Schema
blocks.text: 5. Normalization vs a Properly Split Schema

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438609592-626863117.png
blocks.alt: Normalization vs a Properly Split Schema

blocks.content: The fix for all three anomalies is the same, split the data so each fact is stored in exactly one place, customer information lives in a customers table, product information lives in a products table, an order row simply references both through foreign keys, covered in the earlier Foreign Key topic.
6. The Normal Forms as a Progressive Sequence
blocks.text: 6. The Normal Forms as a Progressive Sequence

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438610000-665739258.png
blocks.alt: The Normal Forms as a Progressive Sequence

blocks.content: Normalization is not a single step, it is a sequence of increasingly strict rules, first normal form, second normal form, third normal form, and Boyce Codd normal form, each one covered as its own topic in this module, each form builds directly on the one before it, fixing a progressively more subtle category of redundancy.
7. Normalization Is a Tradeoff, Not a Pure Win
blocks.text: 7. Normalization Is a Tradeoff, Not a Pure Win

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438610001-163560288.png
blocks.alt: Normalization Is a Tradeoff, Not a Pure Win

blocks.content: Splitting data across more tables to eliminate anomalies means more joins, covered in the earlier SQL Joins module, are needed to reconstruct a complete picture, this tradeoff is worth understanding early, later topics in this module, including denormalization, cover exactly when accepting some redundancy back is actually the right call.

blocks.title: Normalization is a means, not an end in itself
blocks.content: The goal is a schema with minimal anomalies and reasonable query complexity, not the highest possible normal form for its own sake, this balance is exactly what the Denormalization topic later in this module explores.
8. Common Mistakes

["Repeating an entity full details across many rows instead of referencing it through a foreign key","Not recognizing an anomaly as a symptom of a deeper redundancy problem in the schema","Assuming normalization is an all or nothing choice rather than a sequence of progressively stricter forms","Normalizing far past the point where it actually helps, adding needless join complexity for no real benefit"]

Not recognizing an anomaly as a symptom of a deeper redundancy problem in the schema
Assuming normalization is an all or nothing choice rather than a sequence of progressively stricter forms

blocks.content: 9. Key Takeaways

["Update, insertion, and deletion anomalies all stem from storing a fact about one entity inside a table meant for a different entity","Normalization is a sequence of increasingly strict normal forms, each fixing a progressively subtler kind of redundancy","Normalization is a genuine tradeoff, fewer anomalies against more joins needed to reconstruct a full picture","The next topic, First Normal Form, covers the very first rule in that sequence, requiring every column to hold a single atomic value"]
items: Update, insertion, and deletion anomalies all stem from storing a fact about one entity inside a table meant for a different entity
Normalization is a sequence of increasingly strict normal forms, each fixing a progressively subtler kind of redundancy
Normalization is a genuine tradeoff, fewer anomalies against more joins needed to reconstruct a full picture
The next topic, First Normal Form, covers the very first rule in that sequence, requiring every column to hold a single atomic value
